newsitem.title: USA: FAA proposes fire equipment rule for cargo holds.
newsitem.headline: FAA proposes fire equipment rule for cargo holds.

text.p: All inaccessible cargo holds in U.S. aircraft should be required to have fire detection and suppression equipment by 2001, the Federal Aviation Administration proposed Tuesday.
The rule proposal came more than a year after ValuJet flight 592 plunged into the Florida Everglades, killing all 110 people aboard, after a fire occurred in the cargo hold.

Under the plan, the equipment, consisting of smoke detectors and a halon gas fire suppression system, would be fitted to Class D cargo holds in nearly 3,000 U.S. passenger aircraft that rely on an airtight seal and a fire-resistant liner as defence against fires.
About 300 all-cargo aircraft would be required to have detection systems and a means to shut off air flow to the cargo compartment.
The FAA said most long-range passenger aircraft already had this equipment and the rules will bring remaining aircraft to that standard.

"By requiring both detection and suppression systems, we are providing the flying public with the best available protection in the unlikely event of a fire," FAA acting administrator Barry Valentine said in a statement.
It was seen as unlikely that halon gas could have extinguished or significantly slowed the fire on the ValuJet flight that was fed by oxygen generators shipped in the hold.
But industry safety experts said fire detectors might have warned the crew earlier and led to an aborted takeoff or an earlier attempt to return to Miami airport.
Airlines agreed to fit the new fire equipment at a December 1996 meeting at the White House.
The National Transportation Safety Board and lawmakers criticised the FAA and the industry for not moving more aggressively to implement the new rules.
The FAA said there will be 90 days for comment once the proposal was published in the Federal Register. An FAA spokeswoman said the agency was looking to produce a final rule by the end of the year.
An industry source said last week the airlines were still willing to start installing the fire equipment before that final rule was issued.
But there had been delays in waiting for the Environmental Protection Agency to issue a waiver for using halon gas and for the FAA to agree to the outline of the rule.

The source, who requested anonymity, said the airlines were working with Boeing to speed up the delivery date of kits for Boeing 727 and 737 aircraft to December of this year from the third quarter of 1998.
Other aircraft types affected by the rule include McDonnell Douglas, Fokker, Lockheed 11011s and Airbus A320s.
The airline industry estimates the cost of the changes will be around $50,000 to $70,000 per aircraft.
